terms.sub: Type I Hypersensitivity: Sensitization and Mediators
clues: Stored preformed inside mast cell and basophil secretory granules complexed with heparin.
Acts on H1 receptors to produce the classic triple response of redness, flare, and wheal.
A vasoactive biogenic amine released within seconds of IgE cross-linking that causes vasodilation, vascular leakage, pruritus, and bronchospasm.

terms.sub: Type I Hypersensitivity: Sensitization and Mediators
clues: A neutral serine protease stored almost exclusively in human mast cell granules.
Peaks in peripheral blood 60 to 90 minutes after an acute systemic allergic event.
The standard diagnostic laboratory biomarker measured to confirm mast cell degranulation in anaphylaxis.
Clinically associated with allergic rhinitis, extrinsic asthma, and atopic dermatitis.
Strongly linked to elevated serum IgE levels and positive skin prick tests to aeroallergens.
A familial, genetically determined predisposition to mount exaggerated IgE-mediated hypersensitivity responses to common harmless environmental antigens.

terms.sub: Type II Hypersensitivity: Mechanisms and Examples
clues: Presents with the clinical triad of pulmonary haemorrhage (haemoptysis), rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and anti-GBM antibodies.
Shows smooth, continuous linear IgG deposition on renal immunofluorescence microscopy.
A Type II hypersensitivity autoimmune disease caused by IgG antibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen.

terms.sub: Type II Hypersensitivity: Mechanisms and Examples
clues: Explains the pathogenesis of acute rheumatic fever following Streptococcus pyogenes pharyngitis.
Occurs when microbial antigens share structural epitopes with host tissue proteins.
Immunological cross-reactivity in which antibodies or T cells generated against an infectious pathogen attack structurally similar self antigens.

terms.sub: Type III Hypersensitivity: Immune Complex Disease
clues: Classically develops 7 to 14 days after infusion of heterologous antitoxin or certain drugs.
Presents with fever, urticarial rash, arthralgias, lymphadenopathy, and low serum C3 and C4.
The prototype systemic Type III hypersensitivity disorder caused by deposition of circulating soluble antigen-antibody complexes in small vessels and glomeruli.

terms.sub: Type III Hypersensitivity: Immune Complex Disease
clues: Peaks 4 to 8 hours after intradermal antigen injection into a host with high pre-existing IgG titres.
Histologically shows acute neutrophil-rich fibrinoid necrosis of dermal blood vessels.
A localized Type III hypersensitivity reaction caused by in situ immune complex precipitation within blood vessel walls.

terms.sub: Type IV Hypersensitivity: Delayed-Type and T-Cell Cytotoxicity
clues: Examples include nickel ions, poison ivy urushiol, and the reactive beta-lactam ring of penicillin.
Too small (<1000 Da) to stimulate an adaptive immune response on its own.
A low-molecular-weight chemical that becomes immunogenic only after covalently binding to a larger host carrier protein.

terms.sub: Diagnostic Testing in Allergy and Hypersensitivity
clues: Applied to intact skin of the upper back under occlusive chambers for 48 hours.
Evaluated at 48 hours and again at 72 to 96 hours for eczematous erythema and vesicles.
The gold-standard epicutaneous diagnostic procedure for identifying causative allergens in Type IV allergic contact dermatitis.
